chapter_title: Concerning the Three Things that are great with Mankind, as they are running all the time, in that they [ ... ]
chapter_note: No cosmological-correspondential substrate is present. The chapter is entirely later institutional material. The 'three things' are social customs (invoking a name, naming children, swearing oaths) observed in Christian practice, then claimed by Mani for his own apostolate. Both sides of every description stay in the social/religious world — no cosmic domain mapping occurs. The enumeration structure is institutional (three marks of a successful apostolate), not cosmological (no five-fold systems, no realm-face-metal-taste correspondences). The Gardner synopsis confirms this is apostolic succession narrative: Mani comparing his influence to Christ's. The editorial fatigue score shows institutional vocabulary appearing in the second half (shift=+1.89), consistent with the apostolic self-assertion in ¶5-6.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic 'Once again he speaks' opening followed by topic introduction about 'Christian people' and 'three things.' No cosmological content — sets up an institutional comparison between Christian and Manichaean apostolic authority. Bridge connective flag correctly fired.

First of three enumerated social customs: invoking Christ's name on constructions. This is an observation about contemporary Christian religious practice, serving the apostolic succession argument. Enumeration structure is institutional (marks of apostolic greatness), not cosmological. No cosmic-domain mapping present.
Second enumerated custom: naming children after Christ. Continues the institutional framework of 'three marks of a great apostle.' Entirely about social/religious practice in the contemporary world.

Third enumerated custom: swearing oaths by Christ's fortune and surety. Completes the three-fold institutional template. 'All these who are under his authority' is a social description, not a cosmic hierarchy.

Mani's apostolic self-assertion: 'I, Manichaios, who sits before you' — first-person apostolic voice. Claims the same three graces for himself. Contains institutional vocabulary: 'the apostolate of my father,' 'my good and useful teachings,' 'people who love me are called of my name.' Pure apostolic succession narrative. The institutional register score (3.7) confirms.

Apostolic boasting ('Who is as great as I in the universe?') and succession claim ('my brothers the apostles who were before me'). Closes with eschatological promise ('inheritors in the new aeon') typical of institutional-exhortatory closures. The substrate score of 4.82 comes from generic cosmic vocabulary ('creation,' 'universe,' 'aeon') used in apostolic narrative context, not in cosmological-correspondential mapping.
